title: Jared's Saudi Payday: $2 Billion from MBS Six Months After Leaving the White House
description_short: Jared's Saudi Payday: $2 Billion from MBS Six Months After Leaving the White House
description_medium: In June 2021, six months after leaving his White House post, Jared Kushner launched private equity firm Affinity Partners in Miami. By October 2021, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund — controlled by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom Kushner had closely cultivated as a White House adviser — committed $2 billion to Affinity Partners despite an internal Saudi advisory panel concluding that the deal was risky: the fund was inexperienced, due diligence was unsatisfactory in all aspects, and Saudi Arabia would bear the bulk of the investment and risk.
description_long: In June 2021, six months after leaving his White House post, Jared Kushner launched private equity firm Affinity Partners in Miami. By October 2021, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund — controlled by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom Kushner had closely cultivated as a White House adviser — committed $2 billion to Affinity Partners despite an internal Saudi advisory panel concluding that the deal was risky: the fund was inexperienced, due diligence was unsatisfactory in all aspects, and Saudi Arabia would bear the bulk of the investment and risk. MBS overruled his own advisers. As of July 2024, Affinity had collected at least $112 million in management fees from Saudi and other foreign investors but had not returned a single dollar of profit to clients. Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden opened a formal investigation, and in October 2024 Democratic lawmakers formally requested a special counsel probe into whether Kushner was functioning as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia.

title: DOJ Threatens Criminal Charges Against State Election Officials Over Voter Rolls
description_short: DOJ Threatens Criminal Charges Against State Election Officials Over Voter Rolls
description_medium: On July 7, 2026, with the November midterms less than four months away, the DOJ Civil Rights Division sent letters to election officials in all 50 states and D.C. warning that they could face criminal charges if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to vote or remain on voter rolls, demanding a response within five days on intended compliance.
description_long: On July 7, 2026, with the November midterms less than four months away, the DOJ Civil Rights Division sent letters to election officials in all 50 states and D.C. warning that they could face criminal charges if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to vote or remain on voter rolls, demanding a response within five days on intended compliance. The letters invoked statutes carrying prison sentences for election officials found to have issued ballots to ineligible voters. Senior DOJ officials had been exploring criminal charges against state election officials as early as July 2025 — not based on new evidence but on ideological pressure. UCLA law professor Rick Hasen described the letters as Trump trying to use whatever levers of power and persuasive power to interfere with how states run the 2026 election. Separately, a federal judge blocked a DOJ grand jury subpoena seeking the names and contact information of every Georgia election worker from the 2020 election, calling the subpoena's breadth staggering.

title: FBI Seizes 700 Boxes of 2020 Fulton County Georgia Ballots
description_short: FBI Seizes 700 Boxes of 2020 Fulton County Georgia Ballots
description_medium: On January 28, 2026 — one week after Trump publicly predicted prosecutions over the 2020 election — FBI agents executed a search warrant at Fulton County's Elections Hub and Operations Center in Union City, Georgia, loading hundreds of boxes of sealed 2020 election ballots, tabulator tapes, ballot images, and voter rolls into trucks.
description_long: On January 28, 2026 — one week after Trump publicly predicted prosecutions over the 2020 election — FBI agents executed a search warrant at Fulton County's Elections Hub and Operations Center in Union City, Georgia, loading hundreds of boxes of sealed 2020 election ballots, tabulator tapes, ballot images, and voter rolls into trucks. Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin reported the FBI sought approximately 700 boxes. The warrant alleged possible violations of federal record-retention and election-integrity statutes, though election experts noted no new evidence of fraud had emerged. Fulton County Commissioner Marvin Arrington called it an unprecedented breach of chain of custody. A federal court denied the county's motion to return the seized materials. The seizure occurred months after a Georgia prosecutor dropped the 2023 state-level election interference case against Trump and 18 co-defendants. The Congressional Research Service noted the seizure was legally unprecedented, characterizing it as the first known instance of federal agents physically seizing sealed election ballots from a certified election.

title: China Stops Buying US Soybeans: Farmers Face Five-Year-Low Prices
description_short: China Stops Buying US Soybeans: Farmers Face Five-Year-Low Prices
description_medium: China — which historically purchased at least a quarter of all US-grown soybeans — effectively stopped buying American soybeans in 2025 as a direct consequence of the trade war. In September 2025, China imported zero soybeans from the US, the first time in seven years that shipments fell to zero; for the first time in over 20 years, China did not buy from the autumn US harvest.
description_long: China — which historically purchased at least a quarter of all US-grown soybeans — effectively stopped buying American soybeans in 2025 as a direct consequence of the trade war. In September 2025, China imported zero soybeans from the US, the first time in seven years that shipments fell to zero; for the first time in over 20 years, China did not buy from the autumn US harvest. Brazil captured an 85.2% share of China's soybean imports, with Chinese crushers booking 8 million metric tons of Brazilian beans for September alone. Chicago soybean futures fell to near five-year lows. In March 2025, China had already suspended soybean import licenses for three major US firms — CHS Inc., Louis Dreyfus Grains, and EGT — and imposed $21 billion in levies on US agricultural products including soybeans, wheat, meat, and cotton. US farmers were storing crops in hopes of a price recovery, delaying cash flow, while tractor makers and agricultural equipment businesses also suffered cascading losses.

title: Don Jr. Texts Mark Meadows a Blueprint to Steal the 2020 Election
description_short: Don Jr. Texts Mark Meadows a Blueprint to Steal the 2020 Election
description_medium: Donald Trump Jr. sent Mark Meadows a message outlining possible ways to contest the election while votes were still being counted in November 2020. The supplied account describes proposals involving state legislatures and Electoral College certification. description_long: On November 5, 2020 — two days after Election Day, while votes were still being counted — Donald Trump Jr. texted White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows a detailed multi-path plan for overturning the election results: It's very simple...We have multiple paths We control them all, outlining strategies to exploit Republican majorities in Senate swing-state legislatures to block Electoral College certification. The text was reviewed by the House January 6 Select Committee and reported by CNN in April 2022. Then, as the Capitol was being stormed on January 6, 2021, Trump Jr. frantically texted Meadows urging his father to act: He's got to condemn this sh*t ASAP, and We need an Oval Office address. He has to lead now. It has gone too far and gotten out of hand — implying he knew his father was watching and failing to respond. The texts established that Trump's own son recognized the violence was real and the president was deliberately failing to stop it.

title: Trump Signs EO 14248 Requiring Citizenship Proof to Register to Vote
description_short: Trump Signs EO 14248 Requiring Citizenship Proof to Register to Vote
description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14248 in March 2025 seeking documentary proof of citizenship for registration using the federal voting form. It also addressed voter-roll reviews, funding conditions, and ballot-receipt deadlines. The action raised disputes over presidential authority and election access; issuing the order did not by itself establish that every requirement became enforceable or survived court challenges.
description_long: On March 25, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14248, Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections, requiring documentary proof of U.S. citizenship — such as a passport or REAL ID — to register to vote using the federal voter registration form. The order also directed DHS and DOGE to review state voter rolls against federal immigration databases, threatened to withhold federal election funding from non-compliant states, and ordered the DOJ to enforce Election Day ballot-receipt deadlines against 18 states that allow postmarked-by-Election-Day mail ballots. The Brennan Center estimated 21.3 million eligible citizens lacked ready access to qualifying documents. Federal courts repeatedly blocked the order's major provisions. U.S. District Judge Denise Casper permanently enjoined most of the order in June 2026, finding Trump lacked constitutional authority over election procedures reserved to Congress and the states. Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold called the order unlawful weaponization of federal power designed to make it harder for voters to push back at the ballot box.

title: Tom Homan Spreads Misleading 600,000 Criminal Immigrants Statistic
description_short: Tom Homan Spreads Misleading 600,000 Criminal Immigrants Statistic
description_medium: Tom Homan claimed that more than 600,000 immigrants with criminal records were in the United States, using the figure to support the administration's enforcement agenda. The supplied account questions that presentation of immigration data. Assessing the claim requires distinguishing charges from convictions and people already in custody from those at liberty, rather than assuming the cited total describes newly arrived offenders.
description_long: Beginning July 7, 2025, Trump's border czar Tom Homan repeatedly claimed at public events — including the Turning Point USA Student Action Summit on July 12 and on Fox News — that over 600,000 illegal aliens with criminal records were walking the streets of this nation. FactCheck.org documented extensive flaws: the 647,572 figure from a 2024 ICE letter to Congress included legal immigrants, not just undocumented ones; approximately one-third (222,141) had only been charged, not convicted; roughly 126,000 had only traffic offenses and 92,000 had only immigration offenses; the data spanned 40-plus years of entrants, not recent arrivals; and an undetermined number were already incarcerated by other agencies. Trump himself had separately claimed Biden let in 13,099 convicted murderers, then shifted to 11,888 murderers — numbers drawn from the same dataset but excluding the 40-year timeframe caveat. Reuters data showed ICE detentions of people with no criminal charges jumped 800% under Trump, from approximately 860 in January to 7,800 by June 2025, undercutting the crime-focused messaging.

description_medium: Tulsi Gabbard revoked security clearances from thirty-seven current or former national-security officials in August 2025, accusing them of politicizing intelligence. description_long: On August 19, 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former national security officials via memo, accusing them without evidence of politicization or weaponization of intelligence. Targeted individuals included career analysts involved in the 2017 intelligence community assessment that Russia interfered in the 2016 election on Trump's behalf, as well as members of Biden's National Security Council. Critically, Gabbard's office failed to coordinate the action with other intelligence agencies. The publicly released list inadvertently exposed the identity of a CIA employee who was undercover and scheduled to take up a post abroad—a potentially career-ending and life-threatening error. NBC News reported September 25, 2025 that the mass revocations also blindsided the Justice Department, which was building a criminal case against former CIA Director John Brennan—and that Gabbard's action labeled potential witnesses as treasonous, undermining the prosecution. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was reportedly furious at the lack of coordination. Legal experts said the move would complicate any future national security prosecutions.

Sater had previously worked as an FBI informant and had a murky relationship with both U.S. intelligence and Russian organized crime. The email was eventually disclosed to investigators and became one of the most vivid pieces of documentary evidence linking Trump's business dealings to Russian political influence.

description_long: A federal judge has rejected a preservationist group’s request to block the Trump administration from continuing construction of a $400 million ballroom where it demolished the East Wing of the White House. U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ruled Thursday that the National Trust for Historic Preservation was unlikely to succeed on the merits of its bid to temporarily halt President Donald Trump’s project. title: Laura Loomer Triggers Mass Purge of National Security Council Staff
description_short: Laura Loomer Triggers Mass Purge of National Security Council Staff

Staff removals followed, raising questions about political influence over national-security personnel decisions. The episode centers on access and the criteria for dismissal; it does not establish that every removed official was disloyal or that Loomer alone determined all departures.
description_long: In early April 2025, far-right activist and conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer visited the Oval Office and presented President Trump with a dossier accusing National Security Council staff of disloyalty to MAGA. Trump, furious, directed National Security Adviser Mike Waltz to fire them on the spot. At least 15 NSC officials were dismissed in the first wave—including senior directors overseeing intelligence, technology, and legislative affairs. By April 24, Reuters confirmed at least 20 firings total, leaving sections overseeing Latin America, legislative affairs, and international organizations largely unstaffed. Loomer, who has promoted QAnon-adjacent theories, openly took credit on social media. On May 23, 2025, a second mass termination swept the NSC as Secretary of State Marco Rubio (by then interim National Security Adviser) fired dozens more staff covering nearly every major geopolitical issue, from Ukraine to Kashmir. The administration aimed to shrink the NSC to just a few dozen people. Former national security officials described the gutting as catastrophic for institutional knowledge and America's ability to coordinate complex foreign policy responses.

title: Death Penalty for the Innocent: Trump's $85,000 Campaign Against the Central Park Five
description_short: Death Penalty for the Innocent: Trump's $85,000 Campaign Against the Central Park Five
description_medium: Trump bought newspaper advertisements calling for the return of the death penalty after the 1989 Central Park jogger attack. The campaign intensified public pressure while five Black and Latino teenagers were accused in the case. Their later exoneration makes the advertisements significant to debates about prejudgment and wrongful accusation, without treating the ads as a court order or a criminal verdict.
description_long: On May 1, 1989, real estate developer Donald Trump spent $85,000 to purchase full-page advertisements in the New York Times, Daily News, New York Post, and Newsday under the headline BRING BACK THE DEATH PENALTY. BRING BACK OUR POLICE! — calling for the execution of five Black and Latino teenagers accused of attacking a jogger in Central Park twelve days earlier. The five boys ranged in age from 14 to 16 and had given confessions they later said were coerced; two juries convicted them in 1990 and they served sentences of six to thirteen years. In 2002, DNA evidence and a confession by serial rapist Matias Reyes definitively exonerated all five men; a New York Supreme Court justice vacated their convictions on December 19, 2002, and the city settled with them for $41 million in 2014. Trump refused to apologize even after the exonerations, telling CNN in October 2016, They admitted they were guilty. The fact that that case was settled with so much evidence against them is outrageous.

title: Signal Chat Burns Israeli HUMINT Source in Yemen
description_short: Signal Chat Burns Israeli HUMINT Source in Yemen
description_medium: Reporting after the Signal-chat disclosure raised concerns that sensitive intelligence from an Israeli source in Yemen had been exposed. The supplied account links those concerns to the publication of messages involving planned U.S. strikes. Exposure of information can endanger sources and intelligence cooperation, but it should be distinguished from confirmed identification, capture, or death of a source, none of which follows automatically.
description_long: The March 2025 Signalgate leak did not merely embarrass the Trump administration—it burned a live human intelligence source. According to CBS News reporting on March 28, 2025, Israeli officials were furious that the Signal chat published by The Atlantic contained sensitive intelligence Israel had provided to the United States from a human intelligence source operating in Yemen. Israel had gathered targeting data from this HUMINT asset and passed it to the U.S. for use in the Houthi strike operation. When Hegseth transmitted that targeting information on Signal—on a channel accidentally including a journalist—the source's intelligence was effectively disclosed. A senior American intelligence official confirmed the compromise to CBS News. The Wall Street Journal separately reported Israeli complaints directly to U.S. officials. National Security Adviser Waltz and other officials insisted no sources or methods were compromised, a claim directly contradicted by U.S. and Israeli intelligence personnel. The incident risked permanently damaging intelligence-sharing cooperation with Israel, a cornerstone of U.S. Middle East strategy, and potentially endangered the life of the HUMINT source.

description_long: Across dozens of executive orders issued in January and February 2025, legal scholars Adam Cox and Trevor Morrison documented that Trump was asserting an unprecedented constitutional theory: that the president holds inherent authority to override, disregard, or suspend Acts of Congress when they conflict with his policy agenda. In immigration orders, Trump claimed invasion authority allowed him to suspend the entire immigration statutory code. Stanford Law Review published an analysis in July 2025 finding the administration had advanced practical and statutory arguments inflected with constitutional considerations suggesting Article II gave the president a preclusive presidential impoundment prerogative. title: Third-Country Asylum Deportations: 17,500 Asylum Seekers Sent to Nations They Have Never Visited
description_short: Third-Country Asylum Deportations: 17,500 Asylum Seekers Sent to Nations They Have Never Visited
description_medium: By May 2026, approximately 17,500 people had been deported to third countries — nations other than their home country — under Trump's unprecedented asylum cancellation campaign, per Third Country Deportation Watch. ICE attorneys filed over 24,000 motions in immigration court to pretermit active asylum cases by routing claimants to countries they had no connection to — including Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala, and Uganda.
description_long: By May 2026, approximately 17,500 people had been deported to third countries — nations other than their home country — under Trump's unprecedented asylum cancellation campaign, per Third Country Deportation Watch. ICE attorneys filed over 24,000 motions in immigration court to pretermit active asylum cases by routing claimants to countries they had no connection to — including Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala, and Uganda. In one documented case, a Russian national and her 4-year-old child were ordered deported to Uganda. An Iranian national detained since December 2024 received a motion to deport him to Uganda four days before his scheduled asylum hearing. In November 2025, the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled immigration judges must decide third-country deportation before reviewing asylum claims, effectively placing the burden on asylum-seekers to prove they fear persecution in countries they've never seen. Roughly 12,300 people withdrew or abandoned asylum claims after receiving a pretermission motion — a 16% abandonment rate. Honduras had only agreed to accept 10 non-Honduran deportees per month, yet over 6,300 non-Hondurans received Honduras deportation orders.

title: Alien Enemies Act Invoked; 261 Deported to CECOT Defying Court Order
description_short: Alien Enemies Act Invoked; 261 Deported to CECOT Defying Court Order
description_medium: Trump used the Alien Enemies Act in March 2025 to remove Venezuelans the administration linked to Tren de Aragua. Deportation flights to El Salvador prompted judicial orders and disputes over whether the government complied. The controversy concerned the statute's reach, the evidence supporting individual designations, and access to review, rather than assuming every person removed had a proven gang affiliation.
description_long: On March 15, 2025, Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — last used during World War II — against Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, declaring it an 'invasion.' The following evening, U.S. District Judge James Boasberg issued a temporary restraining order blocking deportations and verbally ordered planes already in the air to turn back; the administration defied both the verbal and written order, arguing planes had left U.S. airspace before the written ruling at 7:26 PM. A total of 261 people were deported that day — 137 under the Alien Enemies Act and 23 alleged MS-13 members — and transferred to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison at $6 million per year paid to President Bukele. The administration's top lawyers signed a court filing arguing the order 'did not apply' because deportees had already left U.S. territory. Legal experts and three Supreme Court justices warned the government's logic would allow deportation of any person, including U.S. citizens, to foreign prisons without legal consequence as long as it was done before a court could intervene.
notes: Preserved account dates the injunction to the following evening, whereas another assigned account dates the order March 15. Exact flight and order chronology requires the linked record.
